column7: Normal Account: A standard bank account. There are no strict upper limits on how much money you can hold or transfer, but you are usually required to maintain a minimum monthly balance (e.g., ₹1,000 to ₹3,000 depending on your branch location).  Minor Account: An account opened for a child under the age of 18. Because minors cannot legally enter contracts, a parent or legal guardian operates and oversees the account until the child turns 18.Small Account: A highly restricted, basic account meant for people who do not have officially valid KYC documents (like an Aadhaar or PAN card). You can open it with just a photograph and a signature. However, it has strict legal limits: you can never hold more than ₹50,000 in it, you cannot deposit more than ₹1 Lakh total in a single year, and you cannot withdraw more than ₹10,000 in a month.

Former or Survivor: Only the first person named on the account (the "Former") can make transactions while they are alive. The second person can only take control of the account if the first person passes away.

column2: This operates like a credit card for your farm. It is primarily used for the Kisan Credit Card (KCC). The bank gives you a credit limit for your seasonal farming costs (seeds, fertilizer, labor). You can withdraw money when you need it and deposit money when you sell your crop. You only pay interest on the exact amount you withdraw and use, not the total limit.
column3: TL / DL (Term Loan / Demand Loan): This is a traditional loan where you receive a lump sum upfront to make a major purchase (like a tractor, solar pump, land development, or a greenhouse). You pay it back over a fixed number of years (e.g., 3 to 7 years) via monthly, half-yearly, or yearly installments.
column4: OD (Overdraft): A facility linked to your regular savings or current account that allows you to withdraw more money than you actually have in the account, up to a specific limit, to handle brief cash crunches. DOD (Demand Overdraft / Clean Overdraft): An overdraft facility where the bank allows you to draw money on short notice, usually backed by liquid securities (like Fixed Deposits or National Savings Certificates) or as an unsecured credit line for a short period.
column5: Branch: The regular staff sitting inside the bank branch processed your application directly. RMRU (Relationship Manager Rural Business/Utilities): Specialized SBI bank officers whose entire job is to handle large rural and agricultural business loans. FSTO (Field Staff / Field Technical Officer): The bank's field officers. They are the ones who physically travel out to villages, inspect your land boundaries, and verify that your crops are actually growing before approving the loan.
column6: DSA / DSE (Direct Selling Agent / Direct Selling Executive): External contract workers or agencies hired by the bank to find potential loan customers and collect their paperwork directly from their doorsteps. SB-OSS (State Bank One Stop Solution): An internal digital platform or specialized doorstep banking channel utilized by SBI to process rural loans efficiently. BA-code / BA (Business Analyst / Business Correspondent): Also known as Bank Mitras or Customer Service Points (CSPs). These are local villagers or shopkeepers authorized by SBI to offer basic banking services and source applications in areas where there is no physical bank building.
column7: Immovable Assets: Things permanently attached to the earth that cannot be moved without destroying them. Examples: Your agricultural land, residential plots, your house, fixed farm sheds, or an open irrigation well. Movable Assets: Physical property that you own which can be easily shifted from one place to another. Examples: Tractors, harvesters, tillers, livestock/cattle, mobile pump sets, or harvested crops currently stored in your barn. Liquid Assets: Items that are already cash or can be converted into actual cash within 24 to 48 hours without losing their value. Examples: Cash in hand, balances in your savings accounts, Fixed Deposits (FDs), Gold jewelry, or National Savings Certificates (NSC).
column8: Primary Security: This is the direct object or asset being funded by the loan, or the immediate output of it. If you take a tractor loan, the tractor itself is the primary security. If you take a crop cultivation loan, the standing crops in your field serve as the primary security. If you default, the bank seizes this item first. Collateral Security: This is a backup guarantee (usually asked for larger loan amounts) in case the primary security isn't enough to cover the debt. For example, if you mortgage your ancestral land or family home as an extra guarantee for a tractor loan, that land or home is the collateral.
column9: Individual Form (AG-LAF-IND): Used when the loan is being taken by an individual human being, a group of family members, or joint individual farmers. The bank evaluates your personal KYC (Aadhaar, PAN) and your personal household income. Non-Individual Form: Used when the loan is being taken by a registered business entity or organization involved in agriculture. This includes Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs), Partnership Firms, Agricultural Cooperatives, or Private Limited Agri-companies. The bank reviews corporate balance sheets, company registrations, and board resolutions instead of personal household details.
column10: To qualify as a tie-up on this form, it must be a formal, written tri-partite agreement between You (the Farmer), the Bank, and a Corporate Buyer/Processor.

column2: Export-Import Code (commonly called IEC or Importer-Exporter Code) is a mandatory 10-digit identification number issued by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), Ministry of Commerce. Any business in India that intends to import goods/services into the country or export them out must have this code. Post-GST, your IEC number matches your firm’s PAN card, but you still need to register it officially to engage in international trade.
column3: URC (Udyam Registration Certificate) Number: This is issued to formally registered businesses that have standard tax documentation (like a PAN and GSTIN). It officially certifies you as a Micro, Small, or Medium enterprise, making you eligible for lower bank interest rates and priority subsidies. UAC (Udyam Assist Certificate) Number: This is a specialized number meant for informal micro-enterprises (like local street vendors, small artisans, or tiny home-run businesses) who do not have a GST registration. Banks help generate a UAC for these informal units so they can still receive the benefits of Priority Sector Lending (PSL) schemes without full corporate red tape.
column4: Zero Defect Zero Effect Certificatio is a prestigious sustainability ranking given to manufacturing MSMEs by the Government of India. Zero Defect: Means your manufacturing quality is so high that your products have a 0% customer rejection rate. Zero Effect: Means your factory processes have zero negative impact on the environment (you practice proper waste management, energy savings, and eco-friendly operations). Businesses are rated as Bronze, Silver, or Gold. If your business is "ZED Rated," banks view you as low-risk and well-managed, often rewarding you with extra concessions or discounts on loan processing fees and interest rates.
column5: This is a Working Capital facility. Instead of handing you a lump sum of cash, the bank sets up a special account with a specific spending limit (e.g., ₹10 Lakhs). You use it like a business credit card to manage day-to-day cash gaps: buying raw materials, paying utility bills, or funding immediate labor costs. You can withdraw money whenever you need it, and deposit sales cash back into the account. You only pay interest on the exact balance you used day-to-day, not on the entire limit.
column6: This is a traditional, structural loan where the bank gives you a lump sum of cash upfront for long-term investments. It is used strictly to acquire permanent capital assets—such as purchasing heavy machinery, building a factory shed, or buying land for your shop. You pay this fixed amount back over an agreed schedule of years (e.g., 3 to 7+ years) via fixed monthly or quarterly installments (EMIs).
column7: These are Non-Fund Based facilities. The bank does not give you actual cash; instead, it uses its financial reputation to give a safety guarantee to a third party on your behalf. Letter of Credit (LC): Used heavily in trading or buying raw materials (often from overseas). The bank guarantees to your supplier that they will receive full payment on time. If you default on paying the supplier, the bank steps in and pays them, converting it into a loan for you. Bank Guarantee (BG): A promise by the bank that you will fulfill a specific contractual obligation (such as completing a government building contract or delivery project). If your business fails to meet the terms of the contract, the bank pays a penalty fee to the contracting department.
column8: A Proforma Invoice is a preliminary, estimated bill sent by a supplier to you before any goods are officially shipped or manufactured. It acts as a formal quotation outlining the exact product descriptions, quantities, item rates, transport costs, and applicable taxes. When you apply for a machinery or asset loan, the bank demands a proforma invoice to verify the exact cost of the asset before they disburse the loan money directly to the supplier's account.
column9: BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards): The national body certifying safe physical standards (famous for the ISI mark). Who needs it: Manufacturing businesses making electrical goods, consumer electronics, steel products, cylinders, toys, or packaged drinking water.
column10: FPO (Food Products Order): A certification mark mandatory for all processed fruit and vegetable items in India (now regulated via FSSAI guidelines). Who needs it: Food processing startups, pickle/jam factories, packed fruit juices, or preserved food vendors.
column11: ISO (International Organization for Standardization): An international framework certifying top-tier management and environmental systems (like ISO 9001). Who needs it: Export-oriented companies, IT/software firms, large medical facilities, or heavy manufacturing units looking to qualify for international corporate or government contracts.

column2: Form 16 is an official certificate issued by an employer to its employees in India. It serves as a comprehensive tax statement proving how much income you earned over the financial year and exactly how much Income Tax was deducted at source (TDS) from your salary and deposited with the government.
column3: For a loan applicant, providing Form 16 is generally required by banks as primary income proof for salaried individuals to verify steady financial stability, especially if you do not have recent consecutive salary slips.
column4: DSP: Defence Salary Package (for personnel serving in the Indian Army, Indian Navy, and Indian Air Force). PMSP: Paramilitary Salary Package (for personnel serving in Central Armed Police Forces like BSF, CRPF, CISF, ITBP, and SSB). ICGSP: Indian Coast Guard Salary Package (specifically for members serving in the Indian Coast Guard).IGCSP: Indian Coast Guard Salary Package (specifically for members serving in the Indian Coast Guard).
column5: Loan Origination System is the internal computer backend software system used by bank staff. When you hand your physical application to a bank employee, they upload your files into the LOS. The system runs automatic checks on your CIBIL/credit score, validates your eligibility criteria, routes the file to the verification manager, and tracks your loan profile from the moment you apply up until the loan is officially approved.
column6: OCAS (Online Customer Acquisition System): This is the entry-point digital platform used to attract and capture new loan leads. If you apply for a loan online through SBI's website or portal rather than walking into a physical branch, the OCAS software processes your initial submission data to check your instant eligibility. LMS (Loan Management System): This system takes over completely after your loan has been approved and the cash is sent to your account. The LMS tracks your active loan for years: it calculates daily interest, schedules your monthly EMIs, monitors whether your payments are clearing, and keeps track of your remaining loan balance.
column7: PDCs (Post-Dated Cheques): This is a manual, paper-based repayment mode. You physically sign a bundle of bank cheques in advance (e.g., 12 to 36 separate cheques) with each cheque dated for a specific future month (e.g., January 5th, February 5th, etc.) for the exact EMI amount. The bank stores these in a secure vault and drops one cheque into the clearing machine every month. Note: Banks rarely accept PDCs today and prefer digital alternatives.
column8: ECS (Electronic Clearing Service): This is an automated electronic payment method. By signing an ECS mandate, you grant the bank permanent legal permission to automatically pull the exact EMI amount directly from your designated bank account (whether that account is inside SBI or with an entirely different bank) on a fixed date every single month without you needing to do anything manually.

column3: A Power of Attorney is a legal document that allows you (the Principal) to appoint a trusted person (your Agent or Attorney-in-Fact) to sign documents, make decisions, and complete financial transactions on your behalf. It is most commonly used by NRIs (Non-Resident Indians) or individuals who are physically unable to visit the bank branch. By submitting a POA, you permit a designated family member or representative residing in India to sign the actual loan agreement and handle property registration steps for you.
column4: This is a unique 11-character alphanumeric code (combining letters and numbers) assigned by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to identify every single bank branch in the country uniquely. The first four characters represent the bank name (e.g., SBIN for State Bank of India), followed by a zero, and the last six characters identify the specific branch location. It ensures that when your loan amount is disbursed, the electronic money transfer safely hits the correct bank account.
column5: HFC (Housing Finance Company): Non-bank financial corporations that specialize only in housing loans (Examples: HDFC, LIC Housing Finance, PNB Housing Finance). FI (Financial Institution): Large public or private financial bodies or development banks.
column6: RERA is a government body established under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, to protect home-buyers from fraudulent builders, unfair practices, and construction delays. The form asks for the RERA Registration Number of your housing project. Banks generally refuse to fund under-construction properties unless the builder has officially registered the project under RERA, as this registration acts as a stamp of safety and legal clearance.
column7: Normal Sale: The standard, most common transaction. You are buying the property directly from the actual owner or builder via a standard, newly drafted sale deed. POA Sale: You are buying the property from an individual who doesn't personally own it but holds a legal Power of Attorney given to them by the real owner to execute the sale. Gift Deed: The property is being transferred to you as a gift (usually by a close relative) without any cash changing hands. The loan in this context might be for constructing a house on that gifted plot or renovating it. Thru 3rd Party Guarantor: A structure where a third party (outside of the primary buyer and seller) formally promises to step in and secure the smooth execution or backing of the transaction.
column8: Term Deposit: Pledging a standard Fixed Deposit (FD) certificate held with the bank. NSC (National Savings Certificate): A government-backed savings bond available through Indian Post Offices. KVP (Kisan Vikas Patra): Another post office savings certificate that doubles your money over a specific timeframe. Govt. Promissory Note: Secure financial certificates or debt bonds issued directly by the central or state government. Immovable Property: Pledging a completely separate, already-owned asset like a residential plot, a different house, or commercial land. Third Party Guarantee: A legal promise signed by an eligible third person who acts as a guarantor, agreeing to pay back your entire loan if you default.

column4: Term Deposit (Regular): You deposit a large sum of money for a fixed timeframe. The bank calculates interest and pays it out to you dynamically at fixed regular intervals—either monthly or quarterly—into your savings account. At the end of the maturity period, you get your initial principal amount back. This is ideal for individuals looking for a regular payout to cover expenses.
column5: Term Deposit (Re-investment): Often called a Special Term Deposit. Instead of paying you interest every month or quarter, the bank leaves the interest inside the account where it compounds quarterly. When the deposit completes its tenure, you receive the entire accumulated wealth (Initial Principal + Total Compounded Interest) together as a single lump-sum payout.
column6: Annuity Deposit: Think of this as the exact opposite of a loan EMI or a recurring deposit. You hand the bank a large lump sum of money all at once. The bank then pays you back in equated monthly installments over a set period (e.g., 3, 5, or 10 years). Each monthly payout contains a mix of your principal amount plus the interest earned on your remaining balance. By the final month, the account balance hits zero and automatically closes.
column7: Multi Option Deposit (MOD) Scheme feature turns your basic savings account into a dynamic wealth tool. It automatically links your savings account to a fixed deposit system to give you a higher interest rate without freezing your liquidity. You establish a threshold limit (for example, SBI triggers this at ₹50,000). Any extra cash sitting in your savings account that crosses this threshold is automatically "swept out" into a fixed deposit in multiples of ₹1,000 to earn higher interest rates. If you issue a check, pay a bill, or withdraw cash that exceeds the money left in your basic savings account, the system automatically triggers a "reverse sweep." It pulls the exact shortage amount back from your fixed deposit units (in multiples of ₹5,000) to clear the transaction automatically, protecting you from bounced checks or transaction failures.
column8: When the system executes a "Reverse Sweep" to pull money back to cover a shortage in your savings account, it needs a rule to decide which fixed deposit unit to break if you have accumulated multiple ones over the year. The form allows you to choose between two tracking methods: LIFO (Last-In, First-Out): This is the bank's standard default choice. The system automatically breaks your most recent (newest) fixed deposit first. This method is generally preferred because it leaves your older fixed deposits untouched, allowing them to finish their maturity timelines and maximize their compounding interest yield. FIFO (First-In, First-Out): The system breaks your oldest fixed deposit first to cover the shortage. Choosing this means your newly created deposits are preserved, while the ones that have been running the longest are broken up prematurely.

column2: Co-applicant (or Co-borrower): This is usually your parent, spouse, or legal guardian. Because a student generally does not earn an income during their studies, a co-applicant is mandatory for almost all education loans. Their steady financial profile (salary or business income) acts as the primary backup. They are legally equally responsible for paying back the loan from day one. Guarantor: This is an additional third party (like a relative or family friend) who steps in to guarantee the loan. It depends on the loan amount and whether you are offering collateral (like property). For example, under standard government rules, loans up to ₹7.5 Lakhs usually do not require a third-party guarantor. If your loan requires a guarantor, they sign in that capacity, agreeing to repay the debt only if both the student and the co-applicant fail to do so.
column3: You must base your numbers strictly on the official Fee Structure Document issued by your university's admission office. Do not try to guess or extrapolate on your own. Banks are fully aware that tuition or hostel costs can increase by a small percentage year-over-year. If a formal fee hike occurs later, the university will issue an updated demand letter. You can submit this to the bank, and they can adjust the future semester disbursements within the overall approved loan limit. If you win a scholarship mid-way through your course, it is treated as a blessing rather than a confusion. It will count toward your Margin Money (the portion of the educational expense that you are supposed to pay out of your own pocket). The bank will simply adjust your future disbursement amounts downward by the amount of the scholarship, lowering your final loan burden.
column4: SBI Rinn Raksha is a customized group life insurance product explicitly tailored for SBI loan borrowers. It is designed to protect your family from severe financial distress. If an unfortunate event occurs—such as the untimely demise or permanent disability of the student borrower during the loan tenure—the insurance policy steps in and pays off the entire remaining loan balance directly to SBI. This ensures that the grieving parents or co-applicants are not legally chased for the remaining debt. While it is an extra expense (the premium amount can usually be added directly to your loan balance so you don't pay out of pocket upfront), SBI incentivizes borrowers by offering a 0.50% interest rate concession on the education loan if they opt for the Rinn Raksha policy.
column5: The moratorium period is a legal "repayment holiday" or grace period granted to students. It covers the entire duration of your academic course plus an additional 6 to 12 months (or until you get a job, whichever is earlier). During this time, you are legally excused from paying your regular monthly EMIs. Even though you aren't paying EMIs, interest starts accumulating on every single rupee the bank pays out to your college from the very first day. If left completely untouched, this simple interest compounds and undergoes capitalization—meaning the accumulated interest is added to your original loan principal amount at the end of the moratorium, drastically increasing your starting EMI size. If your parent or co-applicant can afford to pay off just the basic simple interest every month while you are studying (Full Interest Servicing), SBI rewards the account with a 1% interest rate concession, which can save you lakhs of rupees over the lifespan of a 15-year loan.
column6: Yes, you need to navigate both. The Vidya Lakshmi Portal is a centralized online gateway created by the Government of India for students to apply for and track education loans digitally. You must log into the portal first, complete the online Common Education Loan Application Form (CELAF), and upload your primary documents. Then, You will then select "State Bank of India" and your preferred branch on the portal. This securely transmits your digital profile straight into SBI’s processing system. The portal is primarily for initial document tracking and government logging. You still need to visit your designated physical SBI branch with this paper application to complete in-person verifications, sign the legal declarations, allow the co-applicant to execute signatures, and execute the final loan agreements.

column2: Think of the Key Fact Statement (KFS) as a "Truth Sheet" or a summary card for your loan. Instead of forcing you to hunt through 30 to 50 pages of complicated legal fine print, the government mandates that banks extract the absolute most important numbers—like exactly how much money you are borrowing, the true cost, and all the fees—and put them on a single, easy-to-read page. Its main purpose is to give you total transparency so you don't get surprised by hidden costs later.

column5: The Loan Amount & Tenure: Is the approved amount (Loan Amount) and the timeline (Loan Term) exactly what you asked for? Interest Rate & Type: Check the exact interest rate percentage. Also, look at the Interest Type—ensure it says "Fixed" if you wanted a locked rate, or "Floating" if it is allowed to change with market rates. The Monthly EMI: Look at the exact EMI payable amount. Make sure this fits comfortably within your monthly household budget. The Fee List: Review the lines for Processing Fee and Stamp duty. The Golden Rule: If a fee line is left blank or says "Nil" on this sheet, the bank is legally banned from charging you that fee later. The Penalties: Look at the Penalty for delayed payments. You need to know exactly how much extra it will cost you if you accidently pay an EMI a few days late.

column2: The maximum limit equivalent to two months' net take-home salary is a completely new, separate credit line allocated specifically for this emergency facility. It does not overwrite, consume, or combine with any existing loan limits or standard overdraft arrangements you might already have running with the bank. It operates independently as a temporary pocket of emergency cash tied directly to the steady, verified monthly salary income deposited into your designated savings account.
column3: Operating on a reducing drawing power basis means your maximum borrowing limit automatically shrinks in equal parts every month as you pay it back, rather than acting like a reusable credit card. For example, if you take a ₹60,000 overdraft for a 6-month timeline, your spending cap starts at ₹60,000. When Month 1 ends and you make your first repayment installment, the bank permanently lowers your spending boundary by ₹10,000 down to ₹50,000. Even if you clear the balance early, you cannot pull that money back out; the overall limit continues to drop month-by-month until your debt hits zero.
column4: MCLR stands for Marginal Cost of Funds Based Lending Rate. It is the internal benchmark floor interest rate below which a bank is legally not allowed to lend money to any customer. This rate is calculated automatically by the bank based on how much it costs them to maintain funds and pay interest on customer deposits. Because this overdraft uses a "6 months MCLR," your interest rate is tied to this baseline and will be reviewed and updated by the bank every six months to match prevailing economic market conditions.
column5: bps stands for Basis Points, which is a standard financial unit of measurement used by banks to describe minor changes or markups in interest rates. One single basis point is equal to exactly 0.01% (one-hundredth of a percentage point). In the context of this form, when the bank charges a rate "above the MCLR," they use bps as a clear, precise way to state their added profit margin without causing rounding confusion. For example, if the bank decides to charge you a premium margin of "250 bps" over a baseline MCLR of 8.50%, your total effective interest rate will be exactly 11.00%.

column2: Under the Bullet Repayment scheme, a borrower does not pay any periodic installments to the bank during the tenure of the loan. Instead, the entire principal loan amount, along with all accumulated interest, is paid back in one single lump sum (the "bullet") at the end of the loan period (e.g., at 3, 6, or 12 months). Conversely, under an EMI-Based scheme, the loan is paid off steadily over a fixed schedule through monthly installments comprising both a portion of the principal amount and the accrued interest, which progressively reduces the total outstanding debt balance until the end of the tenure.
column3: An SBI Realty Gold Loan is a specialized variant designed exclusively for existing SBI Home Loan borrowers to fulfill funding shortfalls or to pay for unexpected property cost increases, stamp duties, and registration charges. The application form mandates the submission of a "Letter from the Builder" (in the case of flat purchases) along with a home loan arrangement letter to ensure that the gold loan proceeds are legally mapped and verified strictly against an active, authorized real estate project transaction rather than being diverted toward speculative or unauthorized uses.
column4: In the application's ornaments table, Gross Weight refers to the total weight of the jewelry when placed on the scale as a whole, whereas Net Weight represents the exact weight of pure, actual gold after subtracting the weight of any non-precious stones, diamonds, beads, or internal structural wax (lac). As a customer, you must leave this entire section completely blank on your application. The bank will call an independent, authorized Gold Appraiser to test and physically weigh your jewelry at the branch, and they will be the ones to calculate, enter, and formally sign off on these metrics.
column5: LTV stands for Loan-to-Value, and a 75% LTV ratio means that the bank is legally capped from extending a credit amount that exceeds 75% of the appraised market value of your pure gold asset. According to the guidelines, the borrower is contractually bound to maintain this 75% baseline throughout the loan tenure. If international gold market prices crash heavily while your loan is active, causing your outstanding debt to breach the 75% margin of your pledged asset's new value, the bank reserves the right to issue an immediate margin call for you to pay down cash or deposit extra ornaments to restore the ratio.
